title: Bài sưu tầm 107 - Passage 1: The Kauri Forests of New Zealand
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 107

The Kauri Forests of New Zealand

Paragraph 1. Soaring above the forest canopies of New Zealand’s northern peninsula, the kauri (Agathis australis) ranks among the most colossal and long-lived coniferous trees on Earth. Surviving specimens can attain trunk diameters exceeding five metres and reach heights of over fifty metres, with individual trees documented to live for more than two millennia. To the indigenous Māori people, the kauri held profound cosmological significance. In Māori mythology, the giant kauri was revered as Tāne Mahuta, the Lord of the Forest, who pushed the sky away from the earth to bring light and life into the world. Māori craftsmen carefully respected living trees, harvesting only fallen timber to construct massive ocean-going war canoes (waka taua) and extracting bark to produce dark pigments for traditional tattooing.

Paragraph 2. The arrival of European settlers in the late eighteenth century radically altered the fate of the kauri forests. British naval expeditions quickly recognised that the immense, straight, and knot-free trunks possessed ideal mechanical properties for ship masts and spars. Throughout the nineteenth century, an aggressive timber trade developed, transforming the northern forests into industrial logging hubs. Because kauri logs were far too heavy to be hauled through steep, roadless terrain by traditional bullock teams, timber companies developed sophisticated hydrological mechanisms. Loggers erected enormous wooden dams across deep river ravines to trap seasonal rainwater. When the reservoirs reached capacity, explosive trip-mechanisms opened the floodgates, unleashing a torrential surge that flushed hundreds of felled logs downstream to coastal sawmills.

Paragraph 3. Beyond the lucrative trade in kauri timber, an equally feverish economic boom emerged centered on kauri gum. This hardened sub-fossil resin, exuded by injured trees over thousands of years, had pooled in subterranean peat layers and ancient swamp soils. Between the 1870s and 1920s, thousands of European and Dalmatian immigrants worked as professional gum-diggers across the northern wilderness. Armed with steel spears to probe the soft marshland and curved spades to excavate detected deposits, they unearthed fossilised resin nodules weighing up to twenty kilograms. Kauri gum became one of New Zealand’s primary exports, serving as an essential raw ingredient in the manufacture of premium varnishes, outdoor paints, and linoleum across industrial Europe and North America.

Paragraph 4. By the mid-twentieth century, uncontrolled logging and exhaustive gum-digging had reduced the virgin kauri forests by more than ninety-five percent, leaving only fragmented reserves. Just as public awareness prompted strict legal protections to safeguard the surviving ancient groves, a silent biological threat emerged. In the early 2000s, botanists documented mature trees experiencing yellowing foliage, dead canopies, and bleeding resin lesions around the lower trunk. Pathologists identified the cause as Phytophthora agathidicida, an invasive, soil-borne pathogen commonly referred to as kauri dieback disease.

Paragraph 5. The pathogen is lethal and currently incurable; its microscopic water-borne spores penetrate the outer bark and kill the internal vascular tissues that transport vital nutrients, effectively starving the tree to death. Because the pathogen spreads almost exclusively through the movement of microscopic soil particles, human foot traffic along popular hiking trails has become the primary vector of infection. In response, biosecurity agencies have established mandatory cleaning stations along forest access paths, requiring hikers to scrub all traces of mud from their footwear and apply chemical disinfectant before entering pristine kauri zones.

groups.title: Questions 8–13
groups.instructions:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 107?
In boxes 8–13 on your answer sheet, write:
TRUE – if the statement agrees with the information
FALSE – if the statement contradicts the information
NOT GIVEN – if there is no information on this

steps: Đoạn 1: "...harvesting only fallen timber to construct massive ocean-going war canoes..." | Distractors: canopies, pigments.
Từ cần điền: canoes.
Đoạn 2: "...possessed ideal mechanical properties for ship masts and spars." | Distractors: spars, logs.
Từ cần điền: masts.
Đoạn 2: "Loggers erected enormous wooden dams across deep river ravines..." | Distractors: sawmills, gates.
Từ cần điền: dams.
Đoạn 3: "Armed with steel spears to probe the soft marshland..." | Distractor: spades.
Từ cần điền: spears.
Đoạn 3: "...serving as an essential raw ingredient in the manufacture of premium varnishes..." | Distractors: paints, linoleum.
Từ cần điền: varnishes.
Đoạn 4: "...identified the cause as Phytophthora agathidicida, an invasive, soil-borne pathogen..." | Distractors: spores, lesions.
Từ cần điền: pathogen.
Đoạn 5: "...requiring hikers to scrub all traces of mud from their footwear..." | Distractors: spores, soil.
Từ cần điền: mud.

q8.text: Some individual kauri trees are known to have survived for over 2,000 years.

steps: Đoạn 1: "...with individual trees documented to live for more than two millennia."
Kết luận: TRUE.

q9.text: British naval officers compensated Māori leaders before felling kauri trees.

steps: Đoạn 2: Nhắc đến việc Hải quân Anh khai thác gỗ, nhưng hoàn toàn không đề cập họ có đền bù tiền cho thủ lĩnh người Māori hay không.
Kết luận: NOT GIVEN.

q10.text: The kauri gum boom ended when synthetic resin alternatives were introduced.

steps: Đoạn 4: Nhắc đến việc khai thác cạn kiệt đến giữa thế kỷ 20, nhưng không nói lý do kết thúc có phải do xuất hiện nhựa nhân tạo hay không.
Kết luận: NOT GIVEN.

q11.text: Kauri dieback disease produces visible symptoms on both the leaves and trunk of affected trees.

steps: Đoạn 4: "...botanists documented mature trees experiencing yellowing foliage [leaves], dead canopies, and bleeding resin lesions around the lower trunk."
Kết luận: TRUE.

q12.text: A vaccine against kauri dieback spores is currently undergoing field trials.

steps: Đoạn 5: "The pathogen is lethal and currently incurable..." → Trái ngược với việc đang thử nghiệm vaccine.
Kết luận: FALSE.

q13.text: Human outdoor recreation has played an active role in spreading kauri dieback disease.

steps: Đoạn 5: "...human foot traffic along popular hiking trails has become the primary vector of infection."
Kết luận: TRUE.
